analogy.p: Imagine a runner who sees a line and is told to stop at it. First there is a delay while they notice and think, during which they keep running at full speed (thinking distance), then they dig in their heels and slow down (braking distance). Run faster and both parts get longer; run on a slippery floor and the slowing takes longer. It breaks down because a runner can lean and adjust their stride, whereas a car's braking force is limited by tyre grip and the brakes.
analogy.t: A runner who must stop at a red line

bullets: **Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.**
**Thinking distance** is the distance the vehicle travels during the driver's **reaction time**.
**Braking distance** is the distance the vehicle travels under the **braking force** until it stops.
The car travels at **constant speed** during the thinking distance and **decelerates** during the braking distance.
Typical road speeds: a car is about 25 m/s (roughly 56 mph); 30 mph is about 13 m/s.
Both distances increase with speed, but not in the same way.
Stopping distances matter for road safety, speed limits and the gap you should leave behind a vehicle.
core.p: When a driver sees a hazard and needs to stop, the car does not stop instantly. It first travels some distance while the driver reacts, and then travels further while the brakes slow it down. The total is the **stopping distance**. The idea is simple but the exam asks for it in many ways: you must define each part, say what changes each part, use data, and do calculations with speed, time and distance.

bullets: Typical reaction time: **0.2 s to 0.9 s**.
Reaction time is **not constant**: it changes with the person's condition.
Factors that increase reaction time: **tiredness**, **alcohol**, **drugs** (some medicines too) and **distractions** such as a mobile phone or loud music.
Factors do not change how well the brakes work; they change the **thinking distance** only.
Distractions mean the driver sees the hazard later, so the car travels further before braking.
Reaction time can be measured with simple tests (ruler drop) or computer-based tests.
Younger, rested, alert drivers usually have shorter reaction times.
core.p: **Reaction time** is the time between a driver (or any person) seeing a stimulus and starting to respond to it, such as pressing the brake. The brain has to process the signal from the eyes or ears, decide what to do, and send nerve signals to the muscles. A typical reaction time is **between 0.2 s and 0.9 s**. It varies from person to person and depends on many factors, which is why different drivers have different thinking distances at the same speed.

bullets: **Thinking distance = speed x reaction time** (s = v t).
Units: speed in m/s, reaction time in s, distance in m.
**Directly proportional to speed**: double the speed, double the thinking distance.
**Directly proportional to reaction time**: tired or drunk drivers have a bigger thinking distance.
Factors: speed, tiredness, alcohol, drugs, distractions.
Not affected by: road condition, tyre or brake condition, mass of the car.
Example: 20 m/s and 0.60 s gives 12 m.
core.h: Thinking distance and what affects it
core.p: During the reaction time the car carries on at its original speed, so the **thinking distance** equals the speed multiplied by the reaction time (distance = speed x time). Doubling the speed doubles the thinking distance, because the car covers twice as much ground in the same reaction time. A longer reaction time also increases the thinking distance. The mass of the car, the road surface and the brakes do not affect thinking distance at all.

bullets: **Speed:** higher speed means a greater braking distance.
**Mass:** for the same braking force, a heavier vehicle has more kinetic energy and a smaller deceleration, so it takes a longer distance to stop.
**Road conditions:** wet, icy, or leaf-covered roads reduce **friction between tyres and road**, so the maximum braking force is lower.
**Condition of tyres:** worn tyres with little tread grip less, reducing the braking force.
**Condition of brakes:** worn or faulty brakes give a smaller braking force.
**Gradient:** driving downhill increases braking distance (gravity helps the car along).
All these change the **braking distance**, not the thinking distance.
core.h: Braking distance and what affects it
core.p: **Braking distance** depends on how fast the car is travelling and how large the braking force is, and the braking force depends on the condition of the car and the road. A larger braking force means a larger deceleration and a shorter braking distance. The key factors are the speed of the vehicle, the mass of the vehicle, the condition of the brakes and tyres, and the road surface (wet, icy or covered with leaves or oil).

bullets: Brakes work by **friction**, which converts **kinetic energy** into **thermal energy**.
**Work done by braking force = kinetic energy lost**: F x d = 1/2 m v2.
Rearranged: braking distance d = (1/2 m v2) / F.
Brake temperature rises; overheated brakes can lose effectiveness.
Wet or icy roads reduce the grip between tyres and road, so the maximum braking force is smaller.
Kinetic energy: **KE = 1/2 m v2** in joules (J), with m in kg and v in m/s.
Link to **energy conservation**: energy is transferred, not lost; it is dissipated to the surroundings.
core.p: When the driver presses the brake pedal, a **braking force** is applied to the wheels (brake pads press against discs or drums). Friction between the pads and the disc does **work**, and the kinetic energy of the car is transferred to **thermal energy** stored in the brakes. The brakes get hot. The car stops when all of its kinetic energy has been transferred. The work done by the braking force equals the kinetic energy lost: **work done = braking force x braking distance** equals **1/2 m v2**.

bullets: **d proportional to v2** for a constant braking force.
Double the speed means **four times** the braking distance.
Triple the speed means **nine times** the braking distance.
Thinking distance is proportional to v (linear), braking distance proportional to v2 (curve).
This is why the stopping-distance graph is a curve, not a straight line.
Link to equation: v2 = u2 + 2 a s gives s = (v2 - u2) / (2 a); final speed v = 0, so s = u2 / (2a) with a as deceleration.
Speed limits near schools are low because the extra braking distance at higher speeds is so large.
core.h: Why braking distance depends on speed squared
core.p: Kinetic energy depends on the **square** of the speed. For a constant braking force F, the work done F x d must equal 1/2 m v2, so the braking distance d is proportional to v2. Doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times bigger, so the braking distance is four times greater. This is a very common Higher tier idea and explains why a small increase in speed greatly increases the danger in an accident.

bullets: From 30 to 60 mph the speed doubles, thinking distance doubles (9 to 18 m) but braking distance almost quadruples (14 to 55 m).
In graph questions, say 'braking distance increases faster than speed' and quote data from the table with units.
Use the data to compare: stopping distance at 70 mph is about four times the stopping distance at 30 mph (96 / 23 = 4.2).
These figures assume dry road, good brakes and tyres, and an alert driver.
On wet or icy roads the braking distance is at least doubled, and may be up to ten times greater on ice.
core.h: Typical stopping distances and reading data
core.p: You should be able to estimate how the stopping distance of a vehicle changes over a range of road speeds. The Highway Code gives typical values for a dry road and an alert driver: at 20 mph the stopping distance is 12 m (6 m thinking and 6 m braking), at 30 mph it is 23 m (9 + 14), at 40 mph 36 m (12 + 24), at 50 mph 53 m (15 + 38), at 60 mph 73 m (18 + 55) and at 70 mph 96 m (21 + 75). Notice the thinking distance rises steadily while the braking distance rises much faster.

bullets: Method: hold the ruler with the 0 cm mark at the top of the thumb and finger, **drop it without warning**, catch it, and record the distance fallen.
Repeat several times and calculate a **mean** to improve reliability.
The ruler falls freely from rest, so distance d = 1/2 g t2; hence **t = sqrt(2 d / g)** (g = 9.8 m/s2).
Example: caught at 20 cm (0.20 m): t = sqrt(2 x 0.20 / 9.8) = 0.20 s.
Control variables: same ruler, same hand, same person dropping, same distance between the fingers, same time of day.
Computer-based tests (pressing a key when a stimulus appears) can measure reaction time more precisely.
To investigate factors, change one factor at a time (such as caffeine or a distraction) and keep others the same.
core.h: Measuring reaction time: the ruler drop test
core.p: A simple way to measure a person's reaction time is the **ruler drop test**. One person holds a ruler vertically so that the 0 cm end is level with the thumb and finger of a second person, who has their hand open and ready. The ruler is dropped without warning and the second person catches it as quickly as they can. The distance the ruler has fallen, read from the scale at the point where it was caught, is used to find the reaction time. The longer the ruler falls, the longer the reaction time.

bullets: **Large braking forces** can cause the brakes to overheat or the wheels to **skid** and the driver to lose control.
In a crash the deceleration is very large because the stopping time is tiny.
Example: a car at 30 m/s stopping in 0.10 s has a deceleration of 30 / 0.10 = 300 m/s2.
Force on a 70 kg passenger: F = m a = 70 x 300 = 21 000 N, which is large enough to cause serious injury.
Safety features (seat belts, air bags, crumple zones) increase the **stopping time**, reducing the deceleration and force.
Higher tier: estimate forces using F = m a with typical masses and speeds.
Acceleration (deceleration) = change in velocity / time taken.
core.p: To stop a vehicle in a short distance needs a **large deceleration**, which needs a **large braking force**. Very large decelerations are dangerous. In an emergency stop the brakes can overheat, the tyres can skid and the driver can lose control. In a crash, the vehicle may stop in a very short time, which means a huge deceleration and very large forces on the passengers, leading to serious injury. Using F = m a with a large a gives a large F.

bullets: **Braking force F = m a** (use the size of the deceleration).
Braking distance with deceleration a: **s = v2 / (2 a)** (since the final speed is 0).
Using energy: **F s = 1/2 m v2**, so s = m v2 / (2 F).
Example: car 1200 kg decelerating at 6.0 m/s2 needs F = 1200 x 6.0 = 7200 N.
Example: 25 m/s and 6.0 m/s2: s = 625 / 12 = 52 m (to 2 sf).
Convert mph to m/s: roughly divide by 2.24 (30 mph is about 13 m/s).
Always show the equation, substitution and units.
core.p: You can calculate braking distance in two ways. If you know the deceleration, use v2 = u2 + 2 a s with final speed zero. If you know the braking force, you can use work done and kinetic energy. In both cases you must use SI units: speed in m/s, mass in kg and distance in m. The deceleration is the size of the acceleration (it is negative in sign), and the braking force is found with F = m a.

bullets: Say clearly **which part** of the stopping distance is affected.
Reaction-time factors: tiredness, alcohol, drugs, distractions mean greater thinking distance.
Friction factors: wet or icy road, worn tyres, worn brakes mean greater braking distance.
Speed: affects both, but braking distance grows as the square of the speed.
Safety: speed limits, keeping a safe gap, ABS brakes, and regular vehicle checks reduce risk.
Link to energy: the braking distance is large when the kinetic energy to be removed is large.
Link to Newton's second law: lower friction means smaller braking force, smaller deceleration, longer distance.
core.h: Safety, speed limits and exam-style reasoning
core.p: Examiners often ask you to 'explain' why stopping distance increases in some situation. The method is to decide whether it changes the thinking distance or the braking distance, give the reason, and state the effect on total stopping distance. Tiredness changes reaction time, so only thinking distance. Wet roads reduce friction, so only braking distance. Higher speed affects both. This shows careful reading of the question and earns the reasoning marks.

exam: 1 mark: state that stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.
1 mark each: give one factor that affects thinking distance (tiredness, alcohol, drugs, distractions) and one that affects braking distance (wet road, worn tyres, worn brakes, speed, mass).
2 marks: 'explain why' needs the factor, the effect on reaction time or friction, and the effect on the distance.
Key phrase: 'reduces the friction between the tyres and the road, so the braking force is smaller and the braking distance is greater'.
Calculation of thinking distance: write distance = speed x time, substitute with units, and give the answer in metres.
3 marks 'describe how to measure reaction time': drop the ruler without warning, record distance caught, repeat and calculate a mean, then use t = sqrt(2d/g).
Graph questions: read values with units, describe the shape (straight line for thinking distance, curve for braking distance) and quote numbers from the graph.
4 marks (Higher): use work done = kinetic energy: F x d = 1/2 m v2 to explain why doubling speed quadruples the braking distance.
Large deceleration questions: use F = m a, then state the danger (brakes overheat, loss of control, injury).
6 mark questions: structure the answer into thinking distance, braking distance and total, give factors with reasons, include data and a conclusion about safety.
Show units in every step: m/s, s, m, kg, N, J.

mistakes.r: Tiredness increases reaction time, so it increases the thinking distance.
A wet road reduces friction between the tyres and road, which increases the braking distance.
mistakes.w: A wet road makes the thinking distance longer.

mistakes.r: Thinking distance doubles but braking distance quadruples, so the stopping distance more than doubles.
mistakes.w: Double the speed doubles the stopping distance.

mistakes.r: That is the thinking distance; the braking distance is the distance after the brakes are applied.
mistakes.w: Braking distance is the distance travelled while the driver reacts.

mistakes.r: For the same braking force, a heavier vehicle has more kinetic energy and decelerates less, so the braking distance is greater.
mistakes.w: Heavy vehicles have a shorter stopping distance because they are stronger.

mistakes.r: Friction transfers kinetic energy to thermal energy in the brakes (and surroundings); energy is conserved.
mistakes.w: The brakes make the car lose energy.

mistakes.r: Convert speeds to m/s (and distances to m) before using equations.
mistakes.w: Using mph in calculations with g or m/s2.

mistakes.r: Large decelerations need very large forces, which can cause skidding, brake overheating and injury.
mistakes.w: Large decelerations are safe because the car stops sooner.

summary: You must know that stopping distance is thinking distance plus braking distance, what factors affect each part, how reaction time is measured, and why large decelerations are dangerous, including the Higher tier idea that braking distance depends on speed squared. It matters because it links forces, energy and motion to everyday road safety.

terms.d: The distance travelled by a vehicle from when the driver sees a hazard to when the vehicle stops; the sum of the thinking distance and the braking distance.
The distance the vehicle travels during the driver's reaction time.
The distance the vehicle travels under the braking force before it stops.
The time taken for a person to respond to a stimulus; typically 0.2 s to 0.9 s.
A negative acceleration; the rate at which an object slows down, measured in m/s2.
The force applied by the brakes (through friction at the wheels) to slow a vehicle down.
A contact force that opposes the relative motion of two surfaces in contact.
The energy of a moving object: 1/2 x mass x speed squared.
The energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance: work done = force x distance.
Energy stored in the internal energy of a substance; the brakes heat up when they transfer kinetic energy.
How fast an object is moving, measured in metres per second (m/s); a scalar quantity.
Two quantities are directly proportional if doubling one doubles the other.
The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object.
A variable kept the same in an investigation so that it does not affect the results.

worked.q: A car travels at 20 m/s. The driver's reaction time is 0.70 s. Calculate the thinking distance. [2 marks]

A car of mass 1200 kg travelling at 25 m/s brakes with a constant deceleration of 6.0 m/s2. The driver's reaction time is 0.80 s. Calculate (a) the thinking distance, (b) the braking force, (c) the braking distance and (d) the stopping distance. [6 marks]

worked.ans: The student is wrong: the braking distance is proportional to speed squared, so doubling the speed makes the braking distance four times greater, not twice.
worked.q: A student says that doubling a car's speed from 25 m/s to 50 m/s will double the braking distance. Use the idea of kinetic energy to explain why the student is wrong. [4 marks]
steps: Work done by the brakes = kinetic energy lost, so F x d = 1/2 m v2.
For the same braking force F and mass m, the distance d is proportional to v2.
Doubling v multiplies v2 by 4, so the braking distance is four times greater.
Example: if d = 52 m at 25 m/s then at 50 m/s d = 52 x 4 = 208 m.
